lessons.title: Virtualization: KVM, QEMU and libvirt
lessons.goal:
Learn the parts of the Linux virtualization stack and what each does, and check what this machine offers.

Why it matters: most cloud servers are virtual machines on KVM. Knowing the layers helps you read `virsh` and QEMU command lines and understand performance and isolation.

setup.note: These steps only read information, except for creating disk image files in a scratch directory.

steps.title: Are we inside a VM?
steps.text: `systemd-detect-virt` tells whether this system runs on a hypervisor and which. This machine itself is a **guest** on a cloud hypervisor, so the next question (can it host VMs?) depends on **nested virtualization**.

run.cmd: [ -e /dev/kvm ] && echo '/dev/kvm exists: this machine can run KVM guests' || echo '/dev/kvm is missing: no hardware virtualization available to this machine'
run.output: /dev/kvm is missing: no hardware virtualization available to this machine

steps.title: KVM is part of the kernel
steps.text: **KVM** (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) turns the Linux kernel into a hypervisor. It uses the CPU's virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V, Arm virtualization extensions) so guest code runs directly on the CPU, and exposes `/dev/kvm` to user space. This kernel was built with KVM support:

steps.title: The three layers
steps.text:
- **KVM** (kernel): runs vCPUs and handles memory virtualization. It does not emulate devices.
- **QEMU** (user space): one process per VM. It emulates or paravirtualizes devices (disk, network, console), calls KVM to run vCPUs. A vCPU is a **thread** of that process; guest RAM is memory mapped into it.
- **libvirt** (management): a daemon and API (`virsh`, `virt-manager`, `virt-install`) that defines VMs as XML, manages storage and networks and starts QEMU with the right command line.

run.reason: libvirt is not installed here and this machine has no /dev/kvm

steps.title: Paravirtual devices: virtio
steps.text: Emulating real hardware (an Intel e1000 network card) is slow. **virtio** devices are designed for VMs: the guest driver and QEMU share queues in memory, so I/O needs few exits. Cloud images use `virtio-blk`/`virtio-scsi` disks and `virtio-net`. Inside a guest you can see which devices are virtio:

run.cmd: ls /sys/bus/virtio/devices 2>/dev/null | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "virtio devices on this machine"}'

steps.under: Every sensitive guest action (accessing an unmapped device register, executing a privileged instruction the CPU cannot handle) causes a **VM exit**: the CPU stops the guest and returns to the host. KVM handles some exits itself; others go to QEMU in user space. Fewer exits mean better performance, which is what virtio, vhost-net and hardware features (SR-IOV, IOMMU passthrough) achieve.

steps.title: Container or VM?
steps.text: Choose a **VM** for strong isolation, running a different kernel or OS, or untrusted tenants. Choose **containers** for density and speed when the kernel can be shared. Many platforms combine them: lightweight VMs per container (Kata, Firecracker) give VM isolation with container workflows.

options: Makes the Linux kernel a hypervisor using CPU virtualization extensions
quiz.explain: It runs vCPUs; QEMU emulates devices.

quiz.q: What is a vCPU of a QEMU/KVM guest on the host?
options: A thread of the QEMU process

quiz.q: Why are virtio devices faster than emulated ones?
options: Guest and host cooperate through shared queues, with fewer VM exits

quiz.q: Which tool is the libvirt command line client?

check.scenario: A cloud VM cannot start nested KVM guests: `/dev/kvm` does not exist. What are your options?
check.answer: Use an instance type/bare-metal shape that exposes virtualization extensions (nested virtualization enabled), or run guests under software emulation (QEMU TCG: very slow), or use containers instead. Check with `systemd-detect-virt`, `ls /dev/kvm`, `lscpu` (virtualization flags) and the provider's documentation.

lessons.title: VM disk images: raw, qcow2, backing files, snapshots
lessons.goal:
Create and inspect virtual disk images with `qemu-img`: sparse files, thin provisioning, copy-on-write overlays and snapshots.

Why it matters: VM and cloud images are files. Understanding formats explains disk space surprises, fast cloning from a base image, and how snapshots work.

setup.note: These steps only read information, except for creating disk image files in a scratch directory.

steps.title: A raw image is a sparse file
steps.text: A **raw** image is the disk byte for byte. As a sparse file it uses space only for blocks written. `virtual size` is what the guest sees; `disk size` is what the host spends.

run.cmd: qemu-img info disk.raw | grep -E '^(file format|virtual size|disk size)' | sed 's/ (.*//'
run.output:
file format: raw
virtual size: 200 MiB
disk size: 1 MiB

steps.title: qcow2: thin provisioning, snapshots, backing files
steps.text: **qcow2** is QEMU's native format. It allocates clusters on demand, supports compression, encryption, internal **snapshots** and **backing files**. The price is metadata overhead and slightly lower speed than raw.

run.cmd: qemu-img create -f qcow2 base.qcow2 200M | sed 's/fmt=qcow2 //; s/lazy_refcounts=off //; s/refcount_bits=16 //'
run.output: Formatting 'base.qcow2', cluster_size=65536 extended_l2=off compression_type=zlib size=209715200 refcount_bits=16

run.cmd: qemu-img info base.qcow2 | grep -E '^(file format|virtual size|disk size)' | sed 's/ (.*//'
run.output:
file format: qcow2
virtual size: 200 MiB
disk size: 196 KiB

steps.title: Put a file system in it and convert
steps.text: We format the raw image with ext4, write a file, and convert it to qcow2: the free space is not copied, so the qcow2 file is far smaller than the virtual size.

run.cmd: mkfs.ext4 -q -F disk.raw; qemu-img convert -f raw -O qcow2 disk.raw disk.qcow2; qemu-img info disk.qcow2 | grep -E '^(virtual size|disk size)' | sed 's/ (.*//'
run.output:
virtual size: 200 MiB
disk size: 1.19 MiB

steps.title: A copy-on-write overlay on a base image
steps.text: A qcow2 file can use another image as its **backing file**: reads of unchanged blocks come from the base, writes go to the overlay. Creating a VM from a template is then instant and costs space only for the differences. The base must never be modified afterwards.

run.cmd: qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b base.qcow2 -F qcow2 overlay.qcow2 > /dev/null; qemu-img info overlay.qcow2 | grep -E '^(backing file|virtual size|disk size)' | sed -E 's/ \(.*//; s#/tmp/lab/#./#'
run.output:
virtual size: 200 MiB
disk size: 196 KiB
backing file: base.qcow2
backing file format: qcow2

steps.title: Snapshots
steps.text: `qemu-img snapshot -c NAME` records the current state **inside** the qcow2 file; `-a` returns to it, `-l` lists. A snapshot is cheap because it only freezes the block map (copy-on-write).

run.cmd: qemu-img snapshot -c before-upgrade base.qcow2; qemu-img snapshot -l base.qcow2 | awk 'NR>2 {print $2}'

run.output: No errors were found on the image.

steps.under: qcow2 maps guest clusters (64 KB by default) to file offsets through two-level tables with reference counts. A snapshot copies the L1 table and increments reference counts; later writes to shared clusters allocate new ones (copy-on-write). A backing-file chain adds one lookup per layer, so long chains slow reads: flatten them with `qemu-img convert`.

run.cmd: rm -f disk.raw disk.qcow2 base.qcow2 overlay.qcow2; echo cleaned

quiz.q: What is the difference between virtual size and disk size?
options: Virtual size is what the guest sees; disk size is what the file uses on the host

quiz.q: What is a qcow2 backing file?
options: A base image that supplies unmodified blocks to an overlay

quiz.q: How do you flatten a long backing chain?
Which format is usually fastest but not thin by itself?

check.scenario: A VM template of 20 GB is cloned 50 times for tests. How do you avoid using 1 TB?
check.answer: Create each VM disk as a qcow2 overlay with the template as backing file (`qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b template.qcow2 -F qcow2 vmN.qcow2`). Each clone uses space only for its changes. Keep the template read-only, and flatten (`convert`) clones that must outlive it.

interview.q: What are KVM, QEMU and libvirt?
interview.a: KVM is the kernel hypervisor using CPU virtualization extensions. QEMU is the user-space VM process emulating devices. libvirt manages VMs, storage and networks through an API and virsh. See [the lesson](#/lesson/40/kvm-qemu-libvirt).
A family of paravirtual devices (disk, network, console, balloon) where guest and host share queues in memory, giving near-native I/O performance.
raw: simple and fast, sparse. qcow2: thin provisioning, snapshots, backing files, compression, encryption, with some overhead. See [the lesson](#/lesson/40/qemu-img-disks).
The CPU stops running the guest and returns control to the hypervisor, for example on a privileged instruction or device access. Fewer exits mean better performance.

interview.q: Containers versus VMs for multi-tenant isolation?
interview.a: VMs isolate with a hypervisor and separate kernels; containers share the host kernel and rely on namespaces, cgroups and LSMs. Untrusted tenants usually need VMs (or microVMs such as Firecracker/Kata).

glossary.def: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: Linux acting as a hypervisor using hardware virtualization.
The user-space emulator and VM process that works with KVM.
A management layer and API for virtual machines.
Paravirtualized device standard for efficient guest I/O.
QEMU's copy-on-write disk image format with snapshots and backing files.
A base image supplying unmodified data to a qcow2 overlay.
A switch from guest to hypervisor caused by an event the guest cannot handle itself.
